name: Milk clarification (milk punch / milk washing)
what_it_does: Acid (and polyphenols) curdle milk casein; the curd bed filters out solids and tannins, leaving a clear, softer, shelf-stable liquid.
when_to_use: Clarified milk punches; milk-washing a spirit or a whole batch; taming tannic or harsh ingredients.
steps: Build the acidic punch or cocktail batch.
Pour the punch into the milk (common modern order) so it curdles evenly; some methods pour milk into the punch.
Leave undisturbed (a starting point is 10-15 minutes) until curds separate from clearing liquid.
Strain through a coffee filter or cheesecloth-lined fine strainer; re-pour the first cloudy runnings through the curd bed until clear.
Optionally refrigerate overnight so remaining fines settle, then decant.

params.milk_to_punch_ratio: about 1:4 (milk = 1/4 of punch volume) per one guide; about 1:5 per another
params.filter: coffee filter or cheesecloth, recirculate first runnings
params.variant_milk_powder: powdered milk needs no acid; the proteins clump on their own in alcohol (PUNCH)
params.variant_coconut_milk: full-fat coconut milk can replace dairy (PUNCH)
params.variant_hotel_pan: wide slotted hotel pan increases surface area and speeds clarification (PUNCH)

safety: Dairy allergen remains a declared allergen even after clarification.
pitfalls: Stirring after curdling breaks the curd bed and clouds the result.
Replace clogged cheesecloth rather than squeezing it.

name: Agar clarification (quick set)
what_it_does: A weak agar gel traps suspended solids; breaking the gel and draining it releases clear liquid. Works on heat-sensitive juice such as lime.
when_to_use: Same-day clarified citrus or fruit juice for carbonated or clear drinks.
steps: Weigh the juice; plan 0.2% agar by weight.
Boil the agar in a small portion of juice (about 1/5) or in water to hydrate it.
Whisk the hot agar into the rest of the room-temperature juice so the juice is never boiled.
Let it set to a loose gel (cool or ice bath).
Break the gel with a whisk and drain it gently through layered cheesecloth; squeeze lightly.

params.example: 1000 g lime juice + 2 g agar; agar hydrated in 200 g heated juice
params.alt_hydration: hydrate agar in 1 part water, add 4 parts room-temp juice
params.variant_agar_freeze_thaw: agar can also be used in freeze-thaw mode; dose not confirmed in this batch

pitfalls: Clarified lime does not keep longer than fresh; use the same day.
Squeezing too hard pushes solids through.

name: Gelatin freeze-thaw clarification
what_it_does: Gelatin network set through the liquid, then frozen; on slow thaw the clear liquid drips out while the gel holds the solids.
when_to_use: Clarifying almost any juice or liquid when there is time (days) and no centrifuge.
steps: Hydrate gelatin in the liquid at about 5 g per kg.
Let it set in the fridge.
Freeze solid.
Thaw in the fridge in a cheesecloth-lined perforated pan over a container; collect the clear drip.
pitfalls: Slow: thawing takes days; yield lower than centrifuge.

name: Centrifuge clarification
what_it_does: High g-force packs solids into a pellet so clear liquid can be decanted; enzymes and fining agents improve yield and clarity.
when_to_use: High-volume clear juices for carbonated cocktails, clear cordials, herb and spice oils, dense purees.
steps: Optionally pre-treat juice with pectinase (Pectinex Ultra SP-L) to break down pectin.
Optionally fine with kieselsol/chitosan: 2 ml kieselsol per L, wait 15 min; 2 ml chitosan per L, wait 15 min; 2 ml kieselsol per L again.
Spin until solids pellet.
Decant or filter the clear liquid.
safety: Balance the rotor and follow the machine's load limits.
pitfalls: g-force and spin time not confirmed in this batch; left null.

name: Fat washing
what_it_does: Fat-soluble flavour moves from melted fat into the spirit; freezing solidifies the fat for removal, leaving flavour and a rounder texture.
when_to_use: Savory or rich notes in stirred drinks: bacon bourbon (Benton's Old Fashioned), brown butter, coconut rum, sesame.
steps: Melt the fat gently.
Stir the liquid fat into room-temperature spirit in a wide-mouth sealable container.
Rest at room temperature, shaking occasionally (a few hours; up to a day in some methods).
Freeze until the fat forms a solid cap (a few hours to overnight).
Lift off the fat and strain through a coffee filter, cheesecloth or Superbag.

params.bacon_pdt_punch: 1.5 oz bacon fat per 750 ml bourbon; 4 h room temp, 2 h freeze
params.bacon_diffords: 60 ml (2 oz) bacon fat per 70 cl bourbon; a few hours to a day, then freeze
params.coconut_example: 3 oz unrefined coconut oil to 10 oz rum (one home source)
params.sesame_oil: strong; start small (about 1/2 tbsp per cup of spirit suggested by one source) and taste
params.small_batch_oil: 15 ml oil per 250 ml spirit (one bartender quoted)

safety: Keep fat-washed spirit refrigerated or strained well; residual fat can go rancid.
pitfalls: Neutral oils need longer contact and more chilling to separate.
Strong fats (sesame, bacon) are easy to overdo.

name: Rapid nitrous infusion (Arnold method)
what_it_does: N2O under pressure forces liquid into the solid; rapid venting makes the gas boil out of the solid and carries flavour into the liquid in minutes.
when_to_use: Fast spirit or bitters infusions with fresh herbs, spices, tea, coffee, turmeric; to-order infusions.
steps: Put solids and liquid in a cream whipper (do not exceed fill line).
Charge with one N2O charger and swirl a few seconds.
Charge a second time and swirl again (for a 0.5 L whipper).
Rest for the recipe's contact time (e.g. about 1-1.5 minutes in published examples).
Vent quickly with the whipper upright over a container, then open and strain.

params.example_earl_grey_vodka: 300 ml vodka, 4 Earl Grey tea bags, 1 charger, 90 s, vent, strain (whipper-seller example)
params.example_cold_coffee: 300 ml cold water, 60 g coarse coffee, 2 chargers, 1 min, vent slowly

safety: Use only N2O cream chargers and a food whipper rated for pressure.
Vent with the nozzle pointing into a container; contents spray.
pitfalls: Venting slowly gives less extraction than fast venting per Arnold's description.
Warm liquid or long times extract bitterness.

name: Sous-vide infusion
what_it_does: Sealed, gently heated infusion speeds extraction without evaporating alcohol or aroma.
when_to_use: Fruit or spice spirits, liqueurs and bitters in hours instead of weeks.
steps: Combine spirit and botanicals in a vacuum bag or sealed jar.
Hold in a water bath at the set temperature.
Chill in ice water, then strain.

params.examples: bourbon + strawberries 57 C (135 F) 2 h; spiced rum + cherries 57 C 4 h; Pimm's + plums/thyme/orange 60 C (140 F) 1 h

safety: Seal well: hot ethanol vapour is flammable and aroma escapes from leaky bags.
pitfalls: Sous-vide infusions tend to extract less bitterness than long cold steeps; adjust time for tannic botanicals.

name: Oleo saccharum
what_it_does: Sugar draws essential oils out of citrus peel by osmosis, forming an aromatic oily syrup.
when_to_use: Punch bases, citrus-forward syrups, super juice pre-step (oleo citrate).
steps: Peel citrus with minimal pith.
Toss or muddle peels with sugar.
Rest at least 1 hour (often several hours to overnight) until the sugar liquefies; vacuum-sealing takes about 4-6 hours.
Remove peels; optionally dissolve residual sugar with the juice or a little water.
pitfalls: Pith adds bitterness.

name: Super juice (Nickle Morris method)
what_it_does: Peel oils are extracted with powdered acids (oleo citrate), then diluted with water and some fresh juice to make a lime/lemon substitute with far higher yield and longer shelf life.
when_to_use: High-volume bars, waste reduction, consistent citrus.
steps: Weigh the peels.
Add powdered acid equal to peel weight (lime: citric 2 : malic 1; lemon: citric only).
Muddle lightly and rest about 1 hour (oleo citrate).
Blend with water and the fruit's juice; fine strain and refrigerate.

params.example_kos: 100 g peels, 45 g citric, 8 g malic, 1 L water (summaries of Kos; not confirmed as his exact figures)
params.yield_claim: up to about 8x juice per fruit (Kos)

safety: Powdered acids are irritants in concentrated form; weigh carefully.
pitfalls: Aroma differs from fresh juice; taste against fresh before switching.

name: Acid adjusting
what_it_does: Add powdered citric, malic (and trace succinic) acid to a less acidic juice or water so it matches lime or lemon acidity.
when_to_use: Replacing lime/lemon with orange, grapefruit or other juices; clear sours; stable acidity for carbonated drinks.
steps: Pick the target: lime about 4% citric + 2% malic (plus trace succinic); lemon mostly citric.
Dissolve the acids into the juice by weight.
Taste and use in place of lime or lemon.

params.oj_to_lime_per_L: 32 g citric + 20 g malic per 1 L orange juice (Arnold, via PUNCH/VinePair)

safety: Handle concentrated acid powders with care.
pitfalls: Acid adjusting changes sourness, not aroma.

name: Cordials
what_it_does: A syrup acidified (usually with citric and/or malic acid) and flavoured, giving a sweet-sour, shelf-stable modifier.
when_to_use: Highballs (about 1 oz cordial + spirit + soda), Gimlets, replacing fresh citrus in batched or clear drinks.
steps: Extract flavour (e.g. muddle sugar into spent citrus husks and rest a few hours to overnight).
Dissolve sugar in water or juice.
Add citric acid for sourness and malic for length and shelf life; adjust to taste.
Strain, bottle, refrigerate.

params.lime_cordial_morgenthaler: 250 g sugar, 240 ml hot water, 45 ml lime juice, 45 ml grated lime peel, 30 ml citric acid; blend 30 s, strain

pitfalls: Without added acid a lime syrup will not match Rose's-style tartness (Morgenthaler).

name: Forced carbonation (bottle cap, rig, keg)
what_it_does: Dissolves CO2 into a cold, clear, pre-diluted cocktail under pressure.
when_to_use: Carbonated cocktails in bottles, highballs without soda dilution, kegged service.
steps: Build the drink with all its dilution added as water (no ice later); use clarified juices only.
Chill the batch as cold as possible (near freezing).
Carbonate: fill a PET bottle leaving headspace, squeeze out air, fit a carbonation cap, charge with CO2 and shake until no more gas is taken up; or carbonate in a keg.
Rest cold, open slowly, serve in a chilled glass.

params.temp: as cold as possible; CO2 far more soluble cold
params.dilution_example: about 20% cold water in a 3 oz stirred cocktail, about 1/2 oz (Morgenthaler bottled)
params.pressure_note: a bottle at 75 F reading 75 psi reads about 50 psi chilled with the same CO2 content (Morgenthaler)

equipment: carbonation cap and PET bottles, or Perlini shaker, or Cornelius keg
safety: Use only pressure-rated PET bottles or kegs and a regulator; do not exceed equipment ratings.
Glass bottles under pressure can burst.
pitfalls: Particulates act as nucleation sites: cloudy juice foams and loses fizz.
Warm liquid will not hold carbonation.

name: Batching and pre-dilution for bottled cocktails
what_it_does: Replaces ice melt with measured water so a batched drink is correctly diluted straight from the fridge or freezer.
when_to_use: Events, service speed, bottled and freezer cocktails.
steps: Scale the spec by volume.
Add water for the dilution the drink would get from ice (serve without further dilution) or less if it will be stirred/shaken over ice.
Bottle, label, chill.

params.fortified_wine_drinks_pct: about 15 of total volume (PUNCH rule of thumb)

pitfalls: Sources disagree widely; freezer drinks get colder than stirred and taste stronger, so dilute more than instinct suggests.
Fresh citrus in batches degrades within hours.

name: Freezer martini
what_it_does: Pre-diluted Martini stored in the freezer; served colder than a stirred drink because dilution comes from measured water, not ice.
when_to_use: Martini service at home or bars (e.g. Maison Premiere).
steps: Combine gin, vermouth and water (filtered or distilled) in a bottle.
Freeze at least 60-90 minutes (usually stored long-term).
Pour straight into a chilled glass.

params.punch_750ml: 500 ml gin, 125 ml dry vermouth, 125 ml water
params.reiner_750ml: 12 oz gin, 3 oz ambrato vermouth, 3 oz dry vermouth, 3.5 oz distilled water

pitfalls: Too little water makes a hot, harsh drink at freezer temperature.

name: Basic (direct) spherification
what_it_does: Alginate in the flavoured liquid gels on contact with a calcium bath, forming a skin; the gel keeps setting inward.
when_to_use: Caviar-style pearls served immediately.
steps: Blend about 0.5% sodium alginate into the flavoured liquid; rest to degas.
Make a calcium bath (about 1% calcium salt in water).
Drip or spoon the liquid into the bath.
Rinse in clean water and serve promptly.

params.calcium_salts: chloride (fast, bitter), lactate or gluconate (less bitter)

pitfalls: Acidic (low pH) or calcium-rich liquids do not work well with direct spherification.
Pearls keep gelling through; serve soon.

name: Reverse spherification
what_it_does: Calcium is in the flavoured liquid and it is dropped into an alginate bath; the skin forms outside only, so spheres stay liquid inside and keep.
when_to_use: Larger liquid-centre spheres; acidic or alcoholic or dairy liquids.
steps: Add a calcium salt (lactate/gluconate) to the flavoured liquid.
Prepare an alginate bath in water and let it degas.
Spoon the liquid into the bath; hold for the set time.
Rinse in clean water.

params.calcium_salt: lactate or gluconate preferred; chloride tastes bitter
params.gel_plateau_seconds: chloride about 100, lactate about 500, gluconate about 2000 (journal study, basic spherification)

pitfalls: Alginate bath percentage not confirmed in this batch; left null.

name: Siphon foams (espuma)
what_it_does: N2O dissolved under pressure in a protein or gel-stabilised liquid expands into foam on dispensing.
when_to_use: Cocktail toppings (sour foams), make-ahead egg-white foams.
steps: Mix the base (e.g. syrup, citrus, egg white or gelatin-stabilised syrup).
Fill a 0.5 L whipper and charge with one 8 g N2O charger.
Shake vigorously (about six times).
Refrigerate at least 40-60 minutes before dispensing onto drinks.
safety: Raw egg white food-safety rules apply.
pitfalls: Warm base gives loose foam.

name: Lecithin airs
what_it_does: Soy lecithin stabilises a very light bubble foam whipped from a thin flavoured liquid.
when_to_use: Aromatic, weightless toppings (citrus, bitters, tea airs).
steps: Blend 0.4-0.6% soy lecithin by weight into the liquid.
Tilt an immersion blender at the surface to pull in air.
Let the foam settle a moment and spoon the top onto drinks.
pitfalls: Too much lecithin gives heavy, soapy bubbles.

name: Cocktail gels and jellies
what_it_does: Set a cocktail or component with agar or gelatin for bites, cubes or garnish.
when_to_use: Edible cocktails, garnishes, jelly shots.
steps: Hydrate agar (boil) or gelatin (bloom, warm) in the non-alcoholic portion.
Add the spirit once the base has cooled somewhat.
Pour into moulds and set cold.

params.gelatin_rule: 1 envelope Knox gelatin per cup of liquid (generic rule)
params.alcohol_note: alcohol, sugar and salt weaken the gel; raise gelling agent for strong mixes

pitfalls: Boiling after adding spirit drives off alcohol.

name: Liquid nitrogen chilling and nitro-muddling
what_it_does: LN2 (-196 C) chills glasses and drinks instantly and freezes herbs brittle so they can be powdered without browning.
when_to_use: Glass chilling, frozen textures, nitro-muddled herbs (e.g. Arnold's basil drinks).
steps: Pour LN2 into the glass, swirl, and discard fully before use.
Nitro-muddle: freeze herbs with LN2, crush to powder, then immediately douse with the spirit; high-proof ethanol stops the browning enzymes.
Let all LN2 boil off completely before any drink is served.
safety: Never serve a drink with liquid nitrogen still in it: in 2012 an 18-year-old in Lancaster, UK, needed her stomach removed after drinking a shot served with LN2.
Cold burns; asphyxiation risk in closed spaces; never seal LN2 in a closed container.
pitfalls: Herbs thaw and brown if not covered with spirit right away.

name: Rotary evaporator (rotovap) distillation
what_it_does: Vacuum lowers boiling points so aromas can be distilled at low temperature without cooking them.
when_to_use: Clear distillates of delicate aromatics (fruit, flowers, tea) in licensed settings; pioneered in bars by Tony Conigliaro.
steps: Load the flask with the spirit/aromatic mixture.
Apply vacuum and gentle bath heat; rotate the flask.
Collect the condensed distillate.
Blend the distillate into drinks.

params.legal_us: Distilling (separating ethanol from a mixture) requires a TTB permit; no personal-use exemption. Redistilling spirits is regulated under 27 CFR Part 19 Subpart L.

safety: Operating an unlicensed still (including rotovap redistillation of alcohol) is illegal in the US.
Vacuum glassware can implode; use shields.

name: Shrubs (drinking vinegars)
what_it_does: Fruit, sugar and vinegar combined into a sweet-sour syrup.
when_to_use: Non-citrus acidity, highballs, zero-proof drinks.
steps: Cold process: macerate chopped fruit with sugar in the fridge until juice is drawn (2-3 days), strain, add vinegar.
Hot process: simmer fruit in syrup, strain, add vinegar.
Rest, taste, adjust.

params.ratio: 1:1:1 fruit : sugar : vinegar as a starting point
params.cold_start: 1 lb fruit, 2 cups sugar, 2 cups vinegar

pitfalls: Hot process tastes cooked/jammy; cold keeps fresh fruit character.

name: Infused syrups: hot vs cold process
what_it_does: Hot extraction is fast and intense (cooked character); cold extraction is slow and keeps fresh, less tannic flavour.
when_to_use: Herb, tea, spice and fruit syrups.
steps: Hot: steep herbs in just-boiled water like tea about 4-5 minutes (delicate basil up to 30 minutes off heat), strain, dissolve sugar 1:1 or 2:1.
Cold: steep in room-temperature or cold water/syrup 12-24 hours, strain.
pitfalls: Hot steeping extracts more tannin; cold gives rounder, fresher profile.

name: Dilution targets: shaken vs stirred
what_it_does: Chilling and dilution are linked; shaken drinks end colder and more diluted than stirred ones.
when_to_use: Designing specs, batching water amounts, predicting final ABV.
steps: Estimate dilution from starting ABV with Arnold's regressions.
Stirred: dilution ratio = -1.21 x ABV^2 + 1.26 x ABV + 0.145 (ABV as decimal).
Shaken: dilution ratio = -1.567 x ABV^2 + 1.742 x ABV + 0.0203 (as quoted in secondary sources; leading sign reported inconsistently).
Add that fraction of water when batching drinks served without ice.

params.rule_note: no single ideal dilution; 25% is an oversimplification (Arnold)

pitfalls: Secondary quotes of the shaken formula differ on the leading sign; verify constants against the book.

sources.locator: Liquid Intelligence (Dave Arnold, W. W. Norton, 2014); cited via secondary search results; chapter/page not verified
